title: Optimism – a very human characteristic

paragraphs.text: We like to think of ourselves as rational, but neuroscience suggests we are more optimistic than realistic. The belief that the future will be better is known as the optimism bias. It exists in every culture and no matter whether a person is extremely wealthy, desperately poor, or somewhere in between, they are just as likely to share it. Age is not a significant factor either.

You might expect optimism to erode under the tide of news about conflict, unemployment, and threats that shape human life. Indeed, negative stories can make us grow pessimistic about the direction of our nation or the ability of leaders to improve education and reduce crime. But optimism about our personal future remains resilient. A survey conducted a decade ago found that while 70% thought families in general were less successful than in their parents’ day, 76% were optimistic about their own family’s future. Overly positive assumptions can make us more likely to ignore stress-related issues at work and less likely to go for medical check-ups, but the bias also keeps us moving forward. To make progress, we must imagine better realities and believe we can achieve them. Recent research has shown that optimists, in particular males, generally work longer hours and earn more. And although they are not less likely to divorce than pessimists, they are more likely to commit to another serious relationship.

Nowadays, a growing body of scientific evidence points to the conclusion that optimism may be hardwired by evolution into the human brain. The science of optimism, once rejected by mainstream scientists as an area worth studying, has opened a new window on the workings of human consciousness. What it shows is fuelling a revolution in psychology, as academics in this field come to acknowledge accumulating evidence that our brains are not just formed by the past but are constantly shaped by the future.

Colleagues have assumed my work on optimism grew out of a keen interest in the positive side of human nature. The reality is, I stumbled onto the brain's innate optimism by accident. After witnessing a fight, I set out to investigate the memories of others who saw the event. I was intrigued by the fact that these people felt their memories were as accurate as a recording, although this was not the case. A survey I conducted showed that 11 months afterwards, individuals’ recollections of their experience were consistent with their initial accounts only 63% of the time. They were also poor at recalling specific aspects of the event, such as the offenders’ physical appearance. Why did this happen?

Scientists studying memory proposed an intriguing answer: memories are susceptible to inaccuracies partly because the neural system responsible for remembering past episodes might not have evolved for memory alone. They claimed the memory system is not designed to perfectly replay events, but rather is designed to flexibly construct scenarios in our minds. As a result, memory also ends up being a reconstructive process with details both deleted and inserted.

To test this, with our team of researchers I decided to record the brain activity of volunteers while they imagined future events, and compare those results with brain patterns I observed when they recalled past events. But something unexpected occurred. Once people started imagining a time yet to come, even banal events looked favourable. I asked one participant to picture a plane ride. ‘I thought of my favourite part, the take off, then the long nap and finally landing and clapping the pilot,’ she responded. No delays, no screaming babies. The world was wonderful.

If all our volunteers insisted on this kind of thinking about their personal destiny, what does that tell us about how our brains have evolved? Optimism starts with an extraordinary human talent: mental time travel, the ability to move back and forth through time and space in one's mind, although most of us take this ability for granted. However, it is easy to see why cognitive time travel was naturally selected over the course of evolution. It allows us to plan ahead, to save resources for times of scarcity, to avoid health risks. The capacity to envision the future also means that we worry about losing loved ones or failing at our job, but research shows most of us are more preoccupied with picturing positive outcomes than negative ones, and when we do contemplate defeat and heartache, we tend to focus on avoidance strategies. Mental time travel also has another interesting effect: in one experiment I asked volunteers to imagine a series of adverse events, such as a broken leg. People perceived an event more optimistically if they had experienced it already, finding ways to highlight the positive within the negative.

Neuroscientist Sara Bengtsson has also devised an experiment that manipulates students’ expectations during a brain scan. To induce expectations of success, she primed them with words such as smart and intelligent before they took a test. To induce expectations of failure, the words were stupid and ignorant. The students performed better after affirmative messages. Examining the data, Bengtsson found the students’ brains responded differently to mistakes they made depending on the priming. When mistakes followed positive words, she observed enhanced activity in the brain region involved in self-reflection. However, when participants were primed with stupid, there was no heightened activity after wrong answers. In this case, it appears the brain expected to do poorly and showed no surprise at errors. In other words, expectations become self-fulfilling.
